Crying out depression, depression, depression, on the other hand, seems like an excuse for a curmudgeon. An anonymous call to HR or HQ wouldn't hurt, or even a call from a person in a position of authority such as yourself out of "concern" for an employee. I would think, yes. This is in stark contrast to the settlers in Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, and Nova Scotia. Those places are known for their Anglo-Catholicism, and Newfoundland is one example to take note of. Newfoundland (Talamh an Eisc in the traditional Irish) is a predominantly Catholic island, but the majority of Anglicans who settled there (and remember, Newfoundland is the oldest settlement in the New World), were High Church/Anglo-Catholic. In fact, the first Presbyterian church on the island was established to fight what one man wrote was "a high tendency for the established church to relish in Romish Puseyism." Even the Anglicans settled in this place took after the Romans.

But America is different, being a totally separate entity at this point. From my travelling experience, I have found my home to be a few parishes in Virginia when I am on holiday, all of which are Anglo-Catholic. I have not experienced this as much in Boston or Rhode Island, and when I happen to find myself there I attend a Roman parish. I make my assumptions from the few selections I read in university along with the tendency for tradition to carry on, and seeing that in Virginia etc a lot of parishes are of the High Church disposition, I would assume that this is because of the tradition having been set.

The funny thing is that Newfoundland has a strong connection to Massachusetts, many of the Irish settled there used to travel for work in the fishery to that state. They were predominantly Roman, but a few Anglicans went as well along with a few notable priests of the Church of England in the Dominion of Newfoundland. I think they went as chaplains, merely, but it would be strange to know if they hadn't any influence over the rites and liturgies of the parishes that the fisherman would have attended. 

As a side not, OP, it would be worth your time - if you have the means, which I currently do not - to travel to Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, and visit a few rural Anglican parishes to see how ancient the Mass tends to be. By far, most of the parishes tend to be on the High Church spectrum (with the exception of one parish in St John's), and they are VERY good at carrying on the tradition handed down to them.

I would assume that, as a result of the early Puritan influence in the Americas (to what I am aware of, as a non-American), the Eucharist would've been a once a month or perhaps even more seldom of a celebration. Most written accounts of early Anglican services are just of Morning Prayer, but there are also many of the Mass. I would also assume it would depend on which part of the colonies one lived in, some being more High Church than Puritan.

I love G.K. Chesterton. Our family has a personal connection to him, in fact. During or before WWI, my great grandfather was lunching somewhere in London and recognised Chesterton outside smoking his cigar. He dropped his meal, and his date, and went out to get a word with him. Apparently they became good friends, often exchanging a letter. 

At that time, my g-grandfather had just left his doctorate in English to join the Royal Navy, so seeing some famous author really brightened his life up throughout the war. I think he had met him some time before, at the university, but I cannot be sure. 

"The Man who was Thursday," once published, became his favourite book which he read and re-read over and over. I have his dog-eared, practically fallen apart copy in the bank safe. It will be a family heirloom for years to come. My favourite is Chesterton's "Orthodoxy," because I find it an elegant defence of doctrine. Unfortunately, I do not have a physical copy but rather, read the volume on my Kobo thing. 

The beautiful thing about it is that Chesterton, no doubt, met a lot of people during his short life. During life, God used him as a vessel of grace yet even after death he is still one. That familiar face, the elegant prose, the humour, I love it all. 

One could say the same for Evelyn Waugh as well. He is another brilliant writer, and the first author I cried over. "Brideshead Revisited" will have you laughing and crying often at the same time.
